title: Why Do Songs Get Stuck in Your Head?

fin.big: Simplified illustrations. One gum study is not a proven cure.
fin.small: Sources: Williamson et al., PLoS ONE (2014); Jakubowski et al., Psychology of Aesthetics, Creativity, and the Arts (2017); Beaman, Powell & Rapley, QJEP (2015); Beaman & Williams, British Journal of Psychology (2009), via BPS Research Digest.

parts: Why does a song get stuck in your head?
Stay for the chewing gum trick, and why its scientist won't call it a cure.
Scientists call it involuntary musical imagery. We call it an earworm.
Researchers say most people get one at least once a week.
The usual trigger is simple: a song you heard recently.
The stickiest songs share a shape: a faster beat, a rise-and-fall tune, one surprising jump.
But the most natural escape plan can backfire.
In one study, thinking of another song to push it out made the first one worse.
Now the gum. In a 2015 study, chewing gum cut those song thoughts by about a third.
But it was one small test. Its lead scientist wants more research.
Good news: most earworms feel neutral or pleasant, and usually fade within a day.
